rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec quarter-point hike ~97%; ECB Dec ~93%; BoE Dec ~82%; BoJ Dec ~85%; BoC Dec ~80%; RBA Dec hold ~99%; US 2-year ~4.69% (+0.06)
rows.read: A December Fed hike stays all but certain, and US bond yields rose again into the weekend. Soft French and Spanish inflation weakened the case for European Central Bank hikes after December, even as Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel argued it might have to do more. The Bank of England, Bank of Japan and Bank of Canada are all still expected to hike in December.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: China industrial profits Oct +20.1% y/y; US goods trade gap Oct −$149.5B (fcst −$135.9B); Germany unemployment +9K (fcst +5K); Canada Q3 current account +C$4.5B (fcst C$9.5B)
rows.read: Chinese factory profits grew at their fastest in five months, good news for Australia. The US goods trade gap widened sharply as imports of artificial intelligence equipment surged, a drag on US growth this quarter. German unemployment rose and Canada's surplus with the world shrank, both small misses.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: France CPI Nov 2.9% y/y (fcst 3.2%); Spain CPI Nov 4.1% (fcst 4.7%), core 2.6%; ECB consumer 12-month expectation 3.5% (from 3.1%); Tokyo core CPI Nov 2.9% (fcst 3.0%)
rows.read: Inflation slowed far more than expected in France and Spain as fuel got cheaper, which weighed on the euro. Euro-area households, though, expect faster price rises over the next year. US and Australian inflation still run hot, keeping their central banks leaning toward higher rates.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.read: US technology shares recovered in a shortened session, so the yen and franc got no help from fear. The Gulf stayed tense as the US disabled another ship trying to break its Iran blockade, and that worry went into gold. Thin holiday trading can make moves look bigger than they are.

rows.figure: Brent January settled $95.44 (−1.2%), up ~3% on the week; Brent February ~$92.57; WTI ~$83.08 (−0.7%); gold ~$3,652 (+2.4%)
rows.read: Oil gave back its morning gain into the weekend but still rose on the week, ahead of a meeting of the OPEC+ oil producers. That leaves the Canadian dollar with steady support. Gold's jump gives the Aussie a lift.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: Hedge funds (CFTC, Nov 17): USD index −1.3K (flipped short), EUR −76.6K, GBP +28.8K, JPY −23.8K, CHF −19.8K, CAD −72.1K, AUD +38.0K, NZD −23.6K; asset managers GBP −104.6K, AUD −182.7K, EUR +147.2K
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Heavy bets against the loonie leave room for a fast unwind if Canadian hike bets keep growing.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: NZ final count: coalition 65 of 130 seats, 66 needed (ABC News); S&P France review Fri Nov 27; US Section 301 tariff proposals on 14 economies, comments due Jan 5 (USTR)
rows.read: New Zealand's final election count left the governing coalition one seat short of a majority, so it must win over a smaller party or face a new vote. France's debts remain a weight on the euro, with S&P due to review its credit rating late on Friday, November 27.
